title: Animal Rescue Shelters
one_liner: Nonprofit and municipal shelters convert public funding, donations and adoption activity into animal intake, care, rehoming and owner-reunification services.
overview: The industry includes nonprofit shelters, rescue groups, humane societies, SPCAs and municipal or contracted animal-control shelters that house, treat, foster, transfer and rehome stray, surrendered, seized and abandoned companion animals. Baseline IBISWorld data put U.S. industry revenue at $3.1 billion in 2020 and forecast $3.5 billion by 2025, while current 2025 public operating data show 5.8 million dogs and cats entering U.S. shelters and rescues, 4.2 million adoptions, and continued pressure from longer dog stays, veterinary shortages and care costs. Demand is supported by high pet ownership, with APPA reporting 95 million U.S. pet-owning households in 2025 and total U.S. pet industry spending of $158 billion in 2025.

key_stats.market_size: $3.5 billion estimated U.S. industry revenue in 2025, based on the 2020 IBISWorld baseline forecast path from $3.093 billion in 2020 to $3.5 billion in 2025
key_stats.growth: 2.6% forecast CAGR for 2020-2025 from the baseline IBISWorld report; 2025 shelter/rescue intakes declined 2% from 2024 while adoptions rose 0.7% from 2024
key_stats.shelter_intake: 5.8 million dogs and cats entered U.S. shelters and rescues in 2025, including 2.8 million dogs and 3.0 million cats
key_stats.adoptions: 4.2 million shelter animals were adopted in 2025, including about 2.0 million dogs and 2.2 million cats
key_stats.euthanasia: 597,000 shelter animals were euthanized in 2025; ASPCA reported euthanasia rates fell to 8% in 2025 from 10% in 2019
key_stats.save_rate: Best Friends reported an 82.5% national shelter save rate in 2025 and 68% of U.S. shelters reaching no-kill status in 2025
key_stats.pet_ownership: 95 million U.S. households owned at least one pet in 2025, according to APPA's 2026 State of the Industry preview
key_stats.pet_spending: U.S. pet industry expenditures reached $158 billion in 2025 and were projected at $165 billion in 2026 by APPA

baseline_2022.market_size: $3.3 billion estimated U.S. revenue in 2022 in 2020 dollars, interpolated from the baseline IBISWorld 2020 revenue of $3.093 billion and 2025 forecast of $3.5 billion
baseline_2022.growth: 2.6% forecast CAGR for 2020-2025 in the baseline file
baseline_2022.establishments: Baseline report projected establishments to grow at a 4.44% CAGR from 2020-2026 from 11,394 establishments in 2020
baseline_2022.employment: Baseline report projected employment to grow at a 3.64% CAGR from 2020-2026 from 67,689 workers in 2020

how_it_makes_money: Most operators are nonprofits or public agencies. Revenue comes from individual donations, bequests, foundation and corporate grants, municipal animal-control contracts, government appropriations, adoption fees, reclaim fees, low-cost veterinary and spay/neuter services, microchipping, boarding or training services, thrift-store or event income, and in-kind pet food, medicine and supply donations. Adoption fees are important for engagement but usually do not cover full animal-care costs, so fundraising and public funding remain the economic core.
cost_structure: The 2025 cost base is labor- and care-heavy: animal care staff, veterinary staff, shelter medicine, spay/neuter, vaccines, food, supplies, transport, facilities, utilities, insurance, software, fundraising and compliance. The 2020 baseline showed wages of $1.104 billion on $3.093 billion of revenue, or about 35.7% of revenue, and a 6.8% margin. In 2026, BLS reported pet services including veterinary prices up 5.1% year over year in June 2026, keeping medical care and outsourced veterinary services a major margin pressure.
major_players: Humane World for Animals, formerly Humane Society of the United States
current_dynamics: 2025 operating demand was not surging by intake volume, but the system remained strained because animals, especially large dogs, stayed longer and required more behavioral and medical support. Shelters are using managed intake, foster placement, same-day adoption, fee-waived events, transfers, field reunification and community-cat programs to raise live outcomes without expanding kennel capacity. Donations were helped by a stronger 2025 giving environment, with Giving USA reporting environment and animal giving up 8.2% in 2025, but public agencies still face uneven municipal budgets and staffing shortages.
whats_growing: Foster-based capacity, no-kill programming, community-cat and return-to-field models, microchipping and lost-pet reunification, data reporting through Shelter Animals Count and Best Friends dashboards, corporate pet-welfare grants, low-cost access-to-care clinics, adoption marketing, transport partnerships, and shelter management software are growing. Cat ownership also supports demand: APPA reported 53 million U.S. cat-owning households in 2025, and its 2025 Dog & Cat Report noted 49 million cat-owning households in 2024, up from 40 million in 2023.
whats_shrinking: Traditional kennel-only sheltering, high-volume euthanasia, unmanaged open intake without capacity planning, private-shelter transfer pulls in some markets, and reliance on adoption fees as a primary funding source are shrinking. Best Friends reported U.S. dogs and cats killed in shelters fell 8.1% in 2025 from 2024, while Shelter Animals Count reported 2025 community intakes down 2% from 2024.
recent_developments: 2025-02-13: The Humane Society of the United States and Humane Society International rebranded as Humane World for Animals.
2026-02-04: Shelter Animals Count released its 2025 annual report, reporting 5.8 million dog and cat community intakes in 2025, down 2% from 2024, and 4.2 million adoptions, up 0.7% from 2024.

2026-04-20: ASPCA and Best Friends announced a multi-year $14 million initiative for LA Animal Services, including more than 20 staffing roles and expanded foster, intake and return-to-owner programs.
2026-06-23: Giving USA reported total U.S. charitable giving of $617.20 billion in 2025, with environment and animal giving up 8.2% in 2025.
2026-07-22: APPA reported 71 million dog-owning U.S. households in 2025 and 53% household dog ownership in its 2026 Dog Report release.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modest growth rather than a demand spike. Revenue should benefit from resilient pet attachment, $165 billion projected U.S. pet spending in 2026, corporate grants and higher donor dollars, but real operating capacity will depend on staffing, veterinary access, municipal contracts and the ability to reduce length of stay. The most successful shelters will grow throughput through foster networks, owner-support programs, return-to-home tools, transfers and targeted adoption campaigns instead of relying only on more physical kennel space.
one_sentence: Animal Rescue Shelters remain a fragmented, mission-driven U.S. industry with 2025 demand volumes broadly stable, adoption outcomes improving modestly, and capacity pressure still concentrated in large dogs, veterinary care, staffing and municipal systems.

title: Antiseptic Manufacturing
one_liner: US antiseptic manufacturers make skin-contact antimicrobial preparations for healthcare, food-service and first-aid use, with demand anchored by medical procedures and infection-prevention protocols.
overview: This industry manufactures antiseptic ampoules, tablets, capsules, vials, ointments, powders, solutions and suspensions used on skin to kill or inhibit microorganisms. The core market is healthcare antisepsis, including preoperative skin preparations, surgical scrubs, prep pads, swabs and first-aid antiseptics. The IBIS baseline excludes non-healthcare alcohol hand sanitizer gels and sprays, which sit in a separate hand-sanitizer category, so current sizing is estimated from the 2022 IBIS base rather than the much larger combined antiseptic-and-disinfectant market. Demand is tied to hospital procedures, outpatient care, senior-population medical use, pharmacies, drug wholesalers, medical-supply distributors and food-handling hygiene requirements.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 estimated US revenue of $1.25 billion, derived from the 2022 IBIS revenue base of $1.138 billion and the 2022-2028 IBIS projected CAGR of 2.46%.
key_stats.growth: 2026 estimated growth of about 2.5% year over year; 2025 estimated revenue of $1.22 billion; 2022-2028 projected CAGR of 2.46%.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022 IBIS profit margin was 6.8%; 2026 margin is estimated around 6%-8% as quality, testing, recall and input-cost pressures offset steady healthcare demand.
key_stats.employment: 2022 IBIS employment was 6,120 workers; 2027 IBIS outlook was 6,883 workers, implying roughly 2.4% annual growth over 2022-2027.
key_stats.establishments: 2022 IBIS establishments were 234; 2027 outlook was for continued growth as small manufacturers and contract packagers enter niche formats.
key_stats.trade: 2022 IBIS exports were $179 million and imports were $682 million; imports equaled 41.6% of domestic demand in 2022, making foreign supply a persistent competitive and sourcing factor.
key_stats.demand_driver: US national health expenditures were $5.3 trillion in 2024 and are projected by CMS to grow 5.4% annually on average over 2025-2034.

baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022 profit margin was 6.8%, down from 8.3% in 2017.
baseline_2022.exports: 2022 exports were $179 million, equal to 15.7% of revenue.
baseline_2022.imports: 2022 imports were $682 million, equal to 41.6% of domestic demand.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue share by active ingredient was isopropyl alcohol 30.2%, ethyl alcohol 29.5%, benzalkonium chloride 11.4%, povidone iodine 10.1%, chloroxylenol 6.3% and other 12.5%.

how_it_makes_money.primary_revenue: Selling finished OTC and professional antiseptic products to drug wholesalers, medical-supply distributors, hospitals, pharmacies, food-service channels and retail brands.
how_it_makes_money.healthcare_products: Higher-value revenue comes from sterile preoperative skin-prep applicators, surgical scrubs, CHG/IPA swabs, povidone-iodine prep solutions and procedure-specific formats used in hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers.
how_it_makes_money.consumer_and_first_aid: Manufacturers sell lower-priced alcohol, benzalkonium chloride and iodine products through pharmacies, mass retail, grocery, e-commerce and first-aid kit suppliers.
how_it_makes_money.contract_and_private_label: Some producers earn revenue through private-label filling, packaging, wipes conversion, ampoule/vial formats and contract manufacturing for healthcare brands and distributors.
how_it_makes_money.exports: Exports contributed $179 million in 2022 and remain a meaningful revenue stream, though dollar strength, overseas health spending and trade policy affect competitiveness.

cost_structure.raw_materials: Purchases are the largest cost category, led by ethyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol, chlorhexidine gluconate, benzalkonium chloride, povidone iodine, surfactants, water-treatment inputs, sterile packaging, wipes, plastics and applicators.
cost_structure.labor: Wages were $118 million in 2022, about 10.4% of 2022 revenue; labor intensity rises for sterile filling, quality assurance, validation and regulated packaging operations.
cost_structure.compliance_and_quality: FDA OTC drug monograph compliance, cGMP systems, microbial testing, stability testing, validation, adverse-event handling and recall readiness are material 2025-2026 costs.
cost_structure.freight_and_packaging: Freight, resin, paper lidding, foil pouches, bottles, caps and applicator components remain important margin variables after the 2020-2022 supply-chain shock.
cost_structure.margin_profile: IBIS estimated 2022 EBIT profit at $77 million, or 6.8% of revenue; 2026 profitability is still constrained by recalls, testing, intermittent shortages and import price competition.

major_players: {'name': 'Becton, Dickinson and Company', 'position': 'Baseline industry leader; BD ChloraPrep and PurPrep compete in sterile surgical and preoperative skin preparation.'}
{'name': 'PDI Healthcare', 'position': 'Important infection-prevention supplier with Prevantics CHG/IPA skin and device antiseptic products, Sani-Hands wipes and healthcare education programs.'}
{'name': 'Solventum', 'position': 'Independent healthcare company spun out of 3M in 2024; sells 3M SoluPrep and Avagard antiseptic products in surgical and healthcare personnel hand-prep channels.'}

{'name': 'Cardinal Health', 'position': 'Distributor and private-label medical-products player; Webcol alcohol prep pads were subject to a 2026 voluntary recall, highlighting quality risk in the channel.'}
{'name': 'Atlantis Consumer Healthcare', 'position': 'Owner of US Betadine consumer antiseptic brands after the 2023 Avrio Health brand acquisition.'}
{'name': 'Medline Industries', 'position': 'Large medical-supply manufacturer and distributor competing in prep pads, skin-prep, wound-care and private-label healthcare consumables.'}
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Procedure volumes, hospital spending and ambulatory care support steady demand, with CMS reporting 2024 national health spending of $5.3 trillion and projecting 5.4% average annual growth over 2025-2034. At the same time, antiseptic producers face tighter scrutiny around OTC monograph status, cGMP quality, microbial contamination, sterile packaging and raw-material resilience. The broader US antiseptic-and-disinfectant market was estimated at $11.04 billion in 2025 and $12.14 billion in 2026, but the IBIS-defined manufacturing niche is far smaller because it excludes many surface disinfectants and non-healthcare sanitizer products.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 hospital and ambulatory-surgery antiseptic demand as utilization remains elevated after the pandemic-era procedure backlog.
2025-2026 CHG plus alcohol surgical skin-prep formats, especially sterile applicators and tinted solutions for standardized operating-room workflows.
2025-2026 device-access disinfection and vascular-access bundles aimed at reducing central-line associated bloodstream infections.
2025-2026 private-label and contract-packaged prep pads, swabs and wipes for medical distributors and pharmacy channels.
2025-2026 quality-differentiated products that can document sterility, persistence, workflow efficiency and compliance with healthcare protocols.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026 pandemic-era excess capacity in commodity hand sanitizer and low-differentiation alcohol rubs.
2025-2026 triclosan-style antibacterial wash positioning, after FDA rules found many older consumer antiseptic wash ingredients not GRASE.
2025-2026 margins for smaller firms without scale in testing, validation, procurement and recall management.
2025-2026 tolerance for nonsterile or poorly documented prep products in higher-risk clinical settings.
2025-2026 import-reliant sourcing strategies where tariffs, inspections, freight volatility or supplier disruptions raise delivered cost.
recent_developments: 2026-06-24: CMS projected national health expenditure growth of 5.4% annually over 2025-2034, supporting medical consumables demand.
2026-06-08: FDA posted BD's voluntary recall of specific ChloraPrep Clear and FREPP applicator lots because of potential fungal contamination.
2026-06: A ResearchAndMarkets/Mordor report estimated the broader US antiseptic-and-disinfectant market at $11.04 billion in 2025 and $12.14 billion in 2026.
2026-03-19: Cardinal Health recalled select Webcol 70% isopropyl alcohol prep-pad lots because of Paenibacillus phoenicis microbial contamination.
2025-09: Solventum communicated intermittent Avagard CHG/ethyl-alcohol hand-antiseptic supply shortages expected from October 2025 to February 2026.
2025-04-02: US reciprocal tariff policy introduced a 10% baseline tariff while exempting pharmaceuticals, increasing uncertainty for imported inputs and finished medical consumables.
outlook: Revenue is expected to keep expanding modestly through 2027, with the 2022 IBIS projection implying about $1.28 billion in 2027 revenue and a 2022-2028 CAGR near 2.46%. Healthcare utilization, older patients, surgical volumes and infection-prevention protocols provide a durable demand base. Growth should be strongest in sterile CHG/IPA skin-prep applicators, povidone-iodine alternatives, vascular-access antisepsis and healthcare workflow formats. The main downside risks are microbial-contamination recalls, raw-material interruptions, import competition, tariff uncertainty, FDA data requirements for active ingredients, and buyers trading down in commodity alcohol products. Profit margins are likely to remain steady rather than expand materially unless input costs normalize and manufacturers can command premiums for sterile, evidence-backed formats.
themes: Mature but medically necessary manufacturing niche
Healthcare utilization as the core demand engine
FDA OTC monograph and cGMP scrutiny
Quality systems as a competitive differentiator

title: Apparel Knitting Mills in the US
one_liner: A small, declining domestic knit-apparel manufacturing niche competes on speed, quality and Made-in-USA positioning against much larger import supply chains.
overview: The industry remains structurally small because most high-volume knit apparel production has shifted offshore, but domestic mills retain a role where short lead times, quality control, lower minimum order quantities, government or institutional sourcing needs, and Made-in-USA branding matter. The 2022 IBIS baseline put industry revenue at $259.8 million after a 3.6% 2022 rebound, while public BLS productivity data for broader NAICS 3151 show nominal sectoral output falling from $1.0277 billion in 2023 to $868.1 million in 2024. In 2025-2026, the core tension is that tariffs and de minimis changes raise landed costs for imported apparel, but weak US apparel manufacturing employment and high domestic labor costs limit how much volume returns to US knitting mills.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimate: about $266.9 million for the IBIS-defined industry, based on the 2022 IBIS revenue baseline of $259.8 million and its 2022-2027 forecast path; broader NAICS 3151 sectoral output was $868.1 million in 2024 per BLS/FRED.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimate: about +0.9% for the IBIS-defined industry forecast path; broader NAICS 3151 nominal sectoral output fell 15.5% in 2024 from $1.0277 billion in 2023.
key_stats.employment: 2022 baseline: 2,137 employees in the IBIS-defined industry; broader US apparel manufacturing employment was 71,800 in July 2026, down from 73,200 in April 2026.
key_stats.pricing: US apparel manufacturing PPI was 141.918 in June 2026, roughly flat month over month after 0.7% growth in April 2026 and 0.1% growth in May 2026.
key_stats.profitability: 2022 baseline EBIT margin was 3.3%, with IBIS expecting 3.8% by 2027 if cotton costs ease.
key_stats.establishments: 2022 baseline: 85 establishments; IBIS forecast for 2027: 78 enterprises.

baseline_2022.growth: Revenue rose 3.6% in 2022 after rising 9.1% in 2021 and falling 10.4% in 2020; five-year CAGR to 2022 was -3.0%.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue mix: gloves, mittens, hats and mufflers 30.9%; sweaters 28.6%; contract knitting 15.8%; shirts 13.3%; outerwear including uniforms 6.7%; other apparel products 4.7%.

how_it_makes_money: Mills earn revenue by knitting apparel from yarns and fibers, knitting fabric and manufacturing finished garments, finishing knit apparel, and taking contract knitting work from brands, apparel manufacturers, wholesalers and institutional buyers that need domestic capacity, fast replenishment or smaller production runs.
cost_structure: The cost base is labor- and input-sensitive: yarn, cotton, synthetic fibers, dyes, trims and packaging are the largest variable purchases; wages are material because automation is limited in garment assembly and finishing; utilities, rent, maintenance and machinery depreciation matter for mill operations; freight, compliance, quality assurance and sales costs are more important for small-batch and branded domestic production. The 2022 IBIS baseline showed thin 3.3% EBIT margins, and 2026 USDA cotton data point to tighter global cotton balances that can pressure fiber costs if mills cannot pass increases through.
major_players: Fragmented regional and contract knitting mills
current_dynamics: Import competition still dominates price-sensitive apparel, but 2025-2026 tariff volatility, removal of de minimis treatment for low-value imports, forced-labor enforcement, and sourcing diversification have made domestic speed and compliance more valuable. At the same time, broader apparel manufacturing output and hours worked weakened in 2024-2025, showing that reshoring talk has not translated into a broad capacity rebound. Domestic mills are best positioned in premium knit accessories, sweaters, replenishment programs, small runs, uniforms, and customers that need verifiable US production.
whats_growing: Premium Made-in-USA knit accessories, beanies, gloves and hats; low-minimum and quick-turn contract knitting; compliance-sensitive supply for brands avoiding forced-labor and tariff exposure; domestic replenishment runs for brands trying to reduce inventory risk; products tied to government, institutional, team, uniform or specialty customers.
whats_shrinking: Commodity knit shirts, underwear, nightwear and outerwear where offshore producers have scale advantages; small mills without differentiated customers; labor-intensive sewing and finishing with little automation; import-dependent programs exposed to 2025-2026 tariff and de minimis disruptions; broad US apparel manufacturing hours, which BLS reported down 9.9% in 2025 for NAICS 315.
recent_developments: 2024: BLS/FRED broader NAICS 3151 sectoral output fell to $868.1 million, down 15.5% from $1.0277 billion in 2023.
2024-09-30: HanesBrands completed the sale of the global Champion business to Authentic Brands Group, simplifying its apparel portfolio.
2025-02-03: CBP issued guidance that additional duties on China-origin imports would apply regardless of value and that covered shipments would not qualify for de minimis treatment.

2025-07-31: DHS announced an executive order suspending duty-free de minimis treatment for low-value shipments from all countries, raising compliance and landed-cost pressure on direct-to-consumer apparel imports.
2026-07-15: USDA projected 2026/27 global cotton mill use at 122.0 million bales, up 2% from 2025/26, while ending stocks were forecast to decline.
2026-07: BLS reported US apparel manufacturing employment at 71,800 and apparel manufacturing PPI at 141.918 in June 2026.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is for a small, uneven industry rather than a broad reshoring boom. Revenue can edge up in nominal terms when import costs rise and brands need local responsiveness, but real volume is constrained by domestic labor costs, limited investment, aging mill capacity and offshore scale. Mills with branded, premium, compliant or fast-turn contract niches should outperform; undifferentiated commodity knitwear producers will keep losing share to importers unless tariffs become both durable and large enough to offset cost gaps.
one_sentence: US apparel knitting mills knit apparel or knit fabric and then manufacture garments such as sweaters, shirts, outerwear, hats, gloves and contract-knit products, with demand shaped by apparel retail cycles, import prices, cotton and synthetic fiber costs, tariffs and nearshoring decisions.

title: Arcade, Food & Entertainment Complexes in the US
one_liner: Arcade-restaurants and indoor entertainment centers are shifting from coin-play nostalgia to higher-ticket food, beverage, group-event and immersive attraction formats.
overview: Operators run indoor venues built around paid arcade games, redemption games, rides and attractions, typically supported by food, beverages, birthday parties, corporate events and group packages. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline defined the industry around amusement arcades and game-focused family entertainment centers, excluding gambling, billiards, miniature golf and larger outdoor amusements. By 2025-2026, the model is more hybrid: Dave & Buster's/Main Event, Chuck E. Cheese, Round1, Andretti and similar concepts use games as a traffic driver while monetizing visits through meals, alcohol where permitted, timed play cards, parties and reservable event space.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $4.6 billion, estimated from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $4.459 billion and its 2022-2027 growth path, cross-checked against 2025 Census/FRED growth for NAICS 7131 amusement parks and arcades.
key_stats.growth: 2025: about +1.5% year over year estimated; NAICS 7131 seasonally adjusted revenue increased from $32.537 billion in 2024 to $33.039 billion in 2025, a +1.5% comparable-industry signal.
key_stats.public_company_signal: Fiscal 2025: Dave & Buster's revenue was $2.1028 billion, down 1.4% from fiscal 2024, with comparable-store sales down 5.0%.
key_stats.demand_context: Q1 2026: Census/FRED NAICS 7131 amusement parks and arcades revenue was $8.680 billion, up 0.8% from Q4 2025.
key_stats.price_pressure: June 2026: BLS food-away-from-home CPI was up 3.4% year over year, keeping venue food costs and menu pricing in focus.

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: game and ride admissions 51.1%, general admissions 18.8%, food and beverages 23.5%, event services 2.5%, other 4.1%.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from prepaid game cards, coin/card arcade play, attraction admissions, timed play passes, food, nonalcoholic beverages, alcohol where licensed, redemption merchandise margins, birthday parties, private rooms, corporate events and full-facility buyouts. Mature chains increasingly treat arcade entertainment as the anchor for longer dwell time and higher per-guest food, beverage and event spending.
cost_structure: The core arcade economics mix high upfront equipment and buildout costs with relatively low direct game-play costs, while the restaurant/event model adds labor, food input, beverage, cleaning, insurance and rent intensity. Dave & Buster's fiscal 2025 mix is a useful public benchmark: entertainment revenue was 62.9% of sales, food and beverage revenue was 37.1%, product costs were 14.3% of revenue, operating payroll and benefits were 25.5%, other store operating expenses were 34.5%, and depreciation and amortization was 13.3%.
major_players: Dave & Buster's Entertainment Inc.: fiscal 2025 revenue of $2.1028 billion; 243 company-owned North American venues at fiscal 2025 year-end, including 179 Dave & Buster's stores and 64 Main Event stores.
Chuck E. Cheese: August 2025 company FAQ cited about 465 company-owned US and Canada locations plus 96 franchised locations across 16 countries.
Round One Entertainment: US mall-based arcade, bowling, karaoke and Spo-Cha entertainment operator with continued US expansion through 2025-2026.
Lucky Strike Entertainment: fiscal 2025 revenue of $1.2013 billion across bowling, food and beverage, and amusement and other; amusement and other revenue was $227.2 million in fiscal 2025.
Andretti Indoor Karting & Games: May 2026 announcement described the Durham, North Carolina opening as its 14th US location, combining karting, arcade games, VR, bowling, dining and events.
current_dynamics: Demand is healthier than in the COVID-19 shock period but uneven. Families and young adults still pay for out-of-home social experiences, yet low- and middle-income consumers are sensitive to menu inflation, game-card pricing and travel costs. Large operators are remodeling stores, adding attractions, refreshing menus and leaning into events to offset weaker comparable traffic. Smaller independent arcades benefit from nostalgia and local nightlife positioning but face higher rent, labor, utilities, insurance and equipment replacement costs.
whats_growing: Food-and-beverage attach rates, alcohol-led adult visits, birthday and corporate event packages, cashless card systems, premium redemption games, VR and motion attractions, indoor karting hybrids, bowling-arcade hybrids, subscription or all-you-can-play offers, and remodeled venues with stronger sports-viewing and group-social layouts.
whats_shrinking: Standalone coin-operated arcade rooms, low-service snack-only models, underinvested legacy cabinets, mall venues with weak traffic, traffic from highly price-sensitive households, and margins at operators unable to pass through food, wage, occupancy and insurance cost increases.
recent_developments: 2025-06-29: Lucky Strike Entertainment reported fiscal 2025 total revenue of $1.2013 billion, up 4.0%, and fiscal 2025 amusement and other revenue of $227.2 million.
2025-06-29: Lucky Strike Entertainment said fiscal 2025 acquisitions added 10 locations for $80.9 million of consideration.
2025-08: Chuck E. Cheese reported about 465 company-owned US and Canada locations plus 96 franchised locations across 16 countries.
2026-02-12: The National Restaurant Association projected 2026 US restaurant and foodservice sales of $1.55 trillion, with persistent cost pressure and cautious consumer spending.
2026-03-31: Dave & Buster's reported fiscal 2025 revenue of $2.1028 billion, down 1.4%, with fiscal 2025 comparable-store sales down 5.0%.
2026-05-14: Andretti Indoor Karting & Games announced its Durham, North Carolina venue as its 14th US location.
outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is modest growth rather than a rapid recovery cycle. Industry revenue should edge higher if employment and disposable income hold up, but real growth will be limited by food-away-from-home inflation, higher operating costs, competition from home gaming and streaming, and cautious household budgets. Winners are likely to be operators that combine fresh attractions, disciplined pricing, strong event sales and efficient restaurant operations; weaker venues with old games, thin food programs or poor locations will struggle.
one_sentence: The US arcade, food and entertainment complex industry remains a discretionary leisure business: post-pandemic traffic has normalized, but growth in 2025-2026 depends on value pricing, private events, food-and-beverage execution and new attractions rather than simple arcade game volume.

title: Art & Office Supply Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A small, mature manufacturing niche where writing, marking and office tools are pressured by digital substitution, import competition and tariff-sensitive supply chains.
overview: The industry manufactures non-paper art and office supplies, including pens, mechanical pencils, wood-cased pencils, crayons, markers, staplers, hand stamps, stamp pads, carbon paper, inked ribbons and similar products. IBISWorld's 2022 baseline placed revenue at $3.437 billion in 2022 and described the industry as declining, with demand eroded by electronic documents, online workflows, virtual learning and import competition. By 2025-2026, the core story is stabilization rather than structural acceleration: school and consumer creative categories remain resilient, office replenishment has improved as workers spend more time in workplaces, but physical writing and desk products remain low-growth categories. Tariffs on China-linked imports, elevated customer bargaining power and retailer inventory discipline are pushing manufacturers toward price actions, supplier diversification, automation, SKU pruning and higher-margin branded or sustainable products.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers buy inputs such as plastic resin, ink, pigments, wood, metal components and packaging, then convert them into branded and private-label writing instruments, art materials, marking devices, staplers and related supplies. Revenue comes from sales to mass merchants, office supply chains, warehouse clubs, supermarkets, stationery wholesalers, education distributors, hobby retailers, business-to-business purchasing channels and direct e-commerce programs. Branded lines such as Sharpie, Paper Mate, EXPO, Mead, Five Star, Swingline, Prismacolor and Crayola typically carry stronger margins than commodity pens, pencils and basic office tools, while private-label and bid-based institutional supply programs compete heavily on price.
cost_structure: Purchases are the largest cost bucket because products depend on resin, plastic components, ink, wood, paperboard packaging, metal parts, imported finished goods and freight. Wages are moderate because assembly and packaging remain labor-relevant, but automation and offshore sourcing reduce labor intensity. Gross margins are pressured by retailer bargaining power, import price competition, tariffs, freight swings and fixed-cost absorption when volume falls. 2025-2026 company reports from ACCO and Newell show cost savings, price increases and supplier moves being used to offset tariffs, inflation and weaker volume.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is mixed. Back-to-school spending and creative supplies support seasonal volume, while office demand is still structurally smaller than before 2020 because hybrid work and digital workflows reduce replenishment of pens, folders, stamps, staplers and other desk items. Tariffs are a near-term cost and inventory-planning shock: ACCO cited tariff-related purchase disruptions and softer demand in 2025, while Newell reported tariff costs but also 2026 pricing and productivity offsets. Retail channels are also changing: more sales are planned and researched online, but value-seeking consumers are using discount stores, promotions and delayed purchasing to manage higher prices.
whats_growing: Higher-margin branded writing instruments, markers, art and creative products, back-to-school supplies, products made with recycled or compostable materials, e-commerce and omnichannel replenishment, and adjacent technology accessories at diversified players such as ACCO are growing or receiving investment in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Commodity office supplies tied to five-day office attendance, carbon paper, inked ribbons, basic desk accessories, low-margin undifferentiated pens and pencils, smaller domestic producers without scale, and wholesale or office-store channels exposed to retailer consolidation are shrinking or under pressure in 2025-2026.
recent_developments: 2025-05-30: IBISWorld published an updated Art & Office Supply Manufacturing in the US report, indicating the industry was still facing stark structural challenges from digital substitution and office-work changes.

2025-07-31: ACCO Brands reported Q2 2025 net sales of $394.8 million, down 9.9% year over year, citing tariff-related customer purchase disruptions and softer demand for consumer and business products.
2025-12-31: Newell Brands' 2025 Learning & Development segment generated $2.691 billion of net sales, down 1.0% from 2024, while its writing portfolio remained a core part of the segment.
2026-01-30: ACCO Brands closed the EPOS acquisition, accelerating its shift toward higher-growth technology peripherals and away from reliance on traditional office products.
2026-03-09: ACCO Brands reported 2025 full-year net sales of $1.525 billion, down 8.5% from 2024, and said softer global demand and tariff-related disruptions weighed on sales.
2026-05-01: Newell Brands reported Q1 2026 Learning & Development net sales of $594 million, up 3.8% year over year, with 2.0% core sales growth and stronger category performance.
outlook: Through 2030, the industry is likely to remain flat to slightly positive in nominal terms and weak in real volume terms. 2026 conditions are better than the 2020-2021 trough because office attendance and school purchasing have normalized, but hybrid work has become embedded and digital workflows continue to replace paper-and-pen use. Manufacturers with strong brands, school-season shelf space, sustainable product claims, flexible sourcing and automation should outperform. Smaller or commodity-focused producers will face tighter margins from imports, tariffs, retailer pressure and declining unit demand. A reasonable near-term base case is low-single-digit nominal revenue growth in 2026 with limited margin upside unless tariff costs ease or branded back-to-school sell-through improves materially.
